2028 Subaru Crosstrek Receives a Mid-Cycle Refresh in CGI, Complete With Fresh Colors Inside-Out
12 photos
Photo: AutoYa Interior / YouTube
The Japanese automaker Subaru has done a few things lately – they just launched the all-new E-Outback (aka Trailseeker in America) in the United Kingdom, costing no less than $65k at the current exchange rate. For Japan, they announced the US-produced Ascent Touring is going to the home market as a special edition, and there was also commotion in the sporty department.
Over there, the fans got a reminder from Subaru that it can do funky things, so the new TY85 manual-equipped WRX STI Sport R recorded more than 1,000 pre-orders at home in Japan in just two days. Sadly, it’s not even a full-blown STI anymore – only looks and acts like one without the extra oomph, actually.
Anyway, back to America, Subaru had a great month of October this year - Subaru of America reported sales were up by six percent to 54k units, with the Crosstrek compact CUV taking the first spot, followed by the larger Forester, both reaching their best-ever sales for the month of October of any year. Year-to-date, Subaru is on the right track to recover from the initial slump, and now it’s down less than one percent compared to last year.
But obviously they need to continue with the good trend in order to come out with a positive result by the end of the year. The Legacy, for example, is on its way out of the model range, and the electric Solterra is down more than 42% while the Impreza has also bottomed out by 41%. No worries, as the rumor mill and the members of the imaginative guild of digital car content creators are ready to give a helping hand.
More precisely, the good folks over at the " AutoYa " info channel on YouTube have a satellite venue dubbed " AutoYa Interior, " which is where all the CGI Subaru action resides, and they have prepared a mid-cycle refresh for the 2028 Crosstrek, the company’s second-most popular nameplate currently.
According to the channel’s host, in 2027 we might see the Subaru Crosstrek get updated for the mid-cycle refresh cycle for the 2028 model year, as the third generation was introduced during the 2024 model year in North America. It could receive new engine options, like the 2.4-liter turbo and even a PHEV option alongside the hybrid, but more importantly, it would sport various exterior and interior enhancements.
Those include modified rear lights, a reworked grille with redesigned headlights and LED daytime running lights for the exterior, along with new alloy wheel options and possibly additional colors. The changes inside are also pretty easy to observe, at least in these renderings: Subaru could introduce a new steering wheel and a reworked cockpit for the driver.
The latter could get a fully digital instrument cluster along with a different infotainment screen which abandons the portrait style for a classic landscape layout and gains new functionality. Of course, the resident virtual artist didn’t miss the chance to showcase new hues, either.

Official LEGO New Glenn Rocket and Jacklyn Landing Barge Set Is Not Sold by LEGO
12 photos
Photo: Blue Origin
Try as I might, I can't remember if I ever came across an official LEGO set that's not distributed by LEGO itself. Yet this is exactly what happens with the Blue Origin New Glenn and Jacklyn set announced this week by Jeff Bezos' space company.
The toy is rather small, as it only needs 550 bricks to come together and form something that looks like the company's star rocket and the barge that was built as a sort of offshore landing pad.
When completed, the set stands 10.5 inches (27 cm) tall, and it seems to detail the two bits of hardware as best it can. By the looks of it, only the New Glenn's two stages are represented, with the fairing missing completely from the picture. The Jacklyn, on the other hand, seems to be complete.
The set is advertised as a limited edition, but we're not told whether it's limited in time or production numbers. You can buy yourself one only on the Blue Origin website by paying $294.95 for it. The waiting time is quite short, with the estimates saying deliveries should begin as soon as the week of November 30.
In real life, the New Glenn rocket that's replicated in LEGO bricks is a two-stage launch vehicle that's built in two versions at the moment, 7x2 and 9x4 – the numbers represent the number of engines fitted on the first and second stages, respectively. A third stage, called GS3, has been announced earlier this month.
Why would anyone want to have a New Glenn LEGO set in their home? Well, one reason would be the fact that this piece of hardware will be heavily involved in future space exploration missions of unprecedented scope and scale.
In its 7x2 incarnation, the New Glenn has been flown three times (not always successfully): first with the Blue Ring Pathfinder demonstrator, then to launch NASA's Escape and Plasma Acceleration and Dynamics Explorers (ESCAPADE) mission to Mars, and finally with a BlueBird 7 satellite on board.
The 9x4, on the other hand, hasn't been flown yet, but it will probably get to work pretty soon. That's because Blue Origin will have to launch a lot of missions in the coming years. It will start next year with the launch of the Blue Moon lander in support of the NASA Artemis program, as well as the Volatiles Investigating Polar Exploration Rover (VIPER) that'll look for water and other volatiles on the Moon.
Then, in 2028, Blue Origin will have to send one or both lunar terrain vehicles (LTV, made by private contractors Lunar Outpost and Astrolab) to the Moon in support of the Artemis landings.
In the foreseeable future, both versions of the New Glenn will be used in parallel, depending on the mission ahead. Stick the landing... one brick at a time! The limited edition New Glenn & Jacklyn LEGO set just touched down, and pre-orders are OPEN! Build the landing platform. Stack the booster. Land the booster right on the deck and bring it to port on your favorite display. Turbo Honda Civic Drags a Dodge Charger SRT Hellcat, and Someone Gets Thrashed After a Little Nap
7 photos
Photo: 3 Pedal Racing / YouTube
We found a new racing-related channel on YouTube, and they’re showing us a series of cool battles from the latest Streetcar Takeover event at zMax Dragway , located in Concord, North Carolina, adjacent to the Charlotte Motor Speedway.
According to the description, we are going to find here drag racing of both the quarter-mile and 1/8-mile variety, fast street and race cars, performance builds and modifications, plus race-ready action and behind-the-scenes content. However, we’re mostly interested in their coverage of the Streetcar Takeover event at zMax Dragway, of course.
The latter, alongside The Strip at Las Vegas Motor Speedway , is among the few in the world featuring a four-lane configuration, with zMax opening in 2008 directly in the four-lane, all-concrete drag strip format, earning it the nickname "The Bellagio of Drag Strips." On this occasion, of course, only two of the four lanes are in use, though.
The video kicks off with a quick battle to set up the atmosphere between two defunct cars – a Jaguar F-Type Convertible and a Tesla Model S, dressed in classic black versus white attire. As it turns out, these two drivers were probably noobs: one of them ran a red light, possibly the Jaguar; then the Tesla darted out of its lane to try and keep up and also botched the start, but when the driver saw the red light, they slammed the brakes as hard as possible while the Jag started accelerating.
As such, the black Convertible took over the race and won the skirmish with a meager 13.08s pass while the EV came second with 13.27s. No matter, since both were in the wrong, anyway. Next up came the main event of the video – the meeting between a crimson Honda Civic hatchback of the fifth generation variety and a mighty Dodge Charger SRT Hellcat sedan.
These two clearly meant business, but again the situation was put into perspective by the importance of a good reaction time: the little Civic’s driver was subtly more precise (.150 versus .605) and took off like a storm and gained a good advantage during the early lead. It never relinquished it despite the pursuer’s higher trap speed and the “Hellcat got put to sleep by the turbo Civic” with an 11.75s versus 12.23s pass.
Today, the Honda Civic is less of a target for these bonkers aftermarket modifications, sadly. We’re also not used to seeing too many Civic Type Rs at the local quarter-mile dragstrip. The Dodge Charger fans, on the other hand, are waiting for Stellantis to get back on the V8 track with the latest iteration, which is currently only available as a Daytona EV and in Sixpack form with the 3.0-liter twin-turbo Hurricane inline-six under the hood.

I ride e-bikes professionally, regularly testing new bikes and biking gear. I don’t even own a car – I get around almost exclusively on two wheels. So when it comes to important gear like bike locks for my fleet of e-bikes, I’ve become pretty well-versed out of necessity. And after testing out the world’s strongest folding lock, the FoldyLock Elite 110 , I’m more than impressed. If I could only have one lock for my e-bikes, it’d be this one.
Of course, the name of the game in bike theft prevention is to use more than just one lock, and I’m going to return to that idea at the end of this article.
But for now, believe me when I say that this lock is seriously good, to the point that it has become my new primary.
As long and strong as high-quality chain locks, but lighter, quieter, and more compact!
The FoldyLock Elite 110cm is identical in strength and security to the FoldyLock Forever 90cm that I tested a few years ago, yet is 20 cm (8 inches) longer, reaching 110 cm (43 inches).
Advertisement - scroll for more content
The FoldyLock Forever 90 and FoldyLock Elite 110 are the strongest folding locks in the world, confirmed by the premier international lock certification organization ART. These are the only folding locks that have ever achieved a 3-star ART certification. The scale goes up to 5, but 4-star and 5-star certifications are motorcycle-level locks.
To make things even more impressive, the FoldyLock line achieved that ART 3-star rating three years ago, and no other lock company has matched it on a folding lock since.
If one independent and international lock testing association isn’t enough for you, the lock is also Sold Secure GOLD rated, which is just one step below Sold Secure’s highest ever rating for bike locks.
Again, more on that at the end of this article to get you to that last step for top security.
Why a folding lock?
There are a lot of different styles of locks out there, and each has its own advantages and disadvantages. But as someone who rides e-bikes every day as his job, I’ve come to the opinion that a strong folding lock has the best combination of maximizing advantages and minimizing disadvantages.
For starters, folding locks allow you to lock to larger diameter anchors that would be impossible for U-locks (trees, telephone poles, multiple fence bars, etc). They’re more compact than chain locks of comparable security, both in size and weight. They’re significantly stronger than cable locks (when made with quality materials). And they mount more easily to a bike frame than nearly any other lock style, as they fold tightly and usually come with a holster.
Yes, there are disadvantages too. The segments mean they can’t form as close to a circle as a chain, meaning the maximum size of the tree or telephone pole you’re locking to is slightly smaller than for an equal length chain. And they usually aren’t quite as strong as U-Locks made with angle-grinder-resistant materials. But for their size and convenience, they make perhaps the best single style of lock for the best pairing of strength and convenience.
The concrete foundation kept the bike too far away for a U-lock, but the FoldyLock Elite had no problem reaching multiple fence bars
But why the FoldyLock Elite 110 specifically?
Since I began testing the FoldyLock Elite 110 , I’ve been living with it as my main e-bike lock. I test a lot of locks, and most go onto the shelf when I’m done as backups or to give to friends/family. But the FoldyLock Elite 110 has stayed as my new primary lock, and here’s why.
First of all, as I mentioned, it’s the strongest folding lock in the world, as confirmed by multiple independent testing organizations. So if you want the advantages of a folding lock, there’s simply none more secure than this.
But beyond that, the FoldyLock Elite 110 is covered by multiple patents, including the specialized protected rivets that prevent nut splitter attacks and that take out any squeaks or rattles that are common in other folding locks. The lock also physically locks into its holster, which keeps it both secure (no bounce-outs) and helps keep it silent during the ride. There’s even a coating on the hardened steel segments to protect my bike frame from scratches and resist corrosion during winter use (plus a shutter on the locking mechanism for additional winter corrosion resistance).
Basically, it seems like the company has taken pretty much all of the learnings from previous locks in their lineup, and applied those lessons to the FoldyLock Elite, making it a perfect combination of strength, security, and convenience.
For these scenarios, the only high-security lock options are a chain or a folding lock
How do I use the lock?
As I mentioned, after my time testing the FoldyLock Elite, I can say for sure that if I could only use one bike lock, it would be this one.
But I don’t just use one bike lock. And I recommend you don’t either, if you can swing it.
We’ve long known that the best way to keep your bike safe from thieves is to use two bike locks. It’s partly for the extra security, and partly for the extra time it takes a thief to work on defeating two locks, meaning they’re more likely to choose a different sucker’s bike to steal.
I always recommend using two different styles of bike locks. Think: folding lock plus U-lock, or U-lock plus chain lock, or chain lock plus cable lock, or cable lock plus folding lock, etc. You get the idea.
My FoldyLock Elite is now my primary lock, and it allows me to lock onto just about everything on the street, from official bike racks to chunky utility poles. For my secondary, I use a SeatyLock Mason 220. This U-lock is actually one step higher-rated by Sold Secure, reaching that testing organization’s Diamond level – its highest level of security rating.
Two good locks are better than one!
When I can lock both the folding lock and U-lock to an anchor, I do it. But sometimes, when I’m forced to lock to something wide like a lamppost, I lock the frame and rear wheel with the FoldyLock Elite 110, then lock the front wheel to the frame with the Mason 220 U-lock, as seen in the photo above.
That keeps both of my wheels and my bike locked. Despite there only being one lock keeping the bike in place to the anchor (lamppost), the second lock adds an extra layer of frustration for a thief and is likely to convince them to just choose the next bike on the sidewalk.
That’s why I always recommend using two different locks, and ideally of different styles. I believe the FoldyLock Elite 110 offers the most advantages, but its few disadvantages are offset by a secondary lock, such as a strong U-lock.
When it comes to mounting, I’ve got the holster mounted onto my fork using the supplied flexible mounting straps.
Normally you’d mount it to one of your bottle mounts, but I only have a single set of bottle bosses on my e-bike’s frame, and they are currently taken up by a water bottle holder (surprise!).
I found that despite adding 1.9 kg or 4.1 lb to the side of my fork, my bike still rides just fine. The advantage of a rigid frame is that there’s not really much change to the unsprung mass since everything is unsprung!
I love riding hands-free in the city, and it did take me a day or two to get used to the slightly altered steering moment, but I can still ride my bike hands-free even with the extra weight there on the side of the fork.
At some point I might shift the holster onto the rear rack or swap it out for my bottle holder in favor of a new bottle spot, but so far it’s working great there and hasn’t caused me any handling issues.
Is the FoldyLock Elite 110 worth it?
When it comes to value, I think the FoldyLock Elite 110 takes the cake here, too. It’s normally priced at an MSRP of $145 , though it’s currently on sale for $119 as part of the Black Friday promotions.
There are many diverging rules of thumb out there regarding how much a lock should cost, often landing at around 10-20% of the cost of your bike. I don’t subscribe to any of those fixed numbers, as it all depends on how much you want to keep your bike, but considering this lock is likely to outlast even your nicest e-bikes for several years, I’d say that even the full price of $145 feels like a steal compared to other top-tier locks that go for $200 or more.
As I said, I test hundreds of bikes and dozens of locks as my day job. I live and breathe bikes. The fact that this lock has become my go-to everyday lock is pretty much all you need to know about how impressive it truly is. It’s a pleasure to live with and use, which means that I actually end up using it.

Porsche Took 1.5 Years to Turn a 911 GT3 Into a One-Off Tribute to the 911 GT1
14 photos
Photo: Porsche
For people living outside China, and not deeply involved in racing, the name Zhuhai International Circuit probably doesn't mean a lot of things. For the locals, though, it represents their first official entry in the world of FIA-certified racing.
The track opened its doors back in 1996, exactly 30 years ago, in Jin Ding town in Zhuhai City, Guangdong Province, China. It did so by hosting an endurance race of the now-defunct BPR Global GT Series. The circuit's first race was won by a Porsche 911 GT1 driven by Emmanuel Collard and Ralf Kelleners.
Chances are few people today remember that, exactly three decades ago, a Porsche GT1 won the very first race on the Chinese track. Some of those who do, though, mostly Porsche China, got together and came up with a one-off Porsche 911 GT3 Tribute to 911 GT1.
Named exactly that, the car was presented this week in Guangzhou as a result of one and a half years of hard work that involved people from Porsche Sonderwunsch and Style Porsche, and Studio F. A. Porsche.
Photo: Porsche Deep down, the car remains its usual GT3 self, with a 4.0-litre naturally aspirated six-cylinder boxer engine as its heart. It beats at 503 horsepower and 450 Nm of torque, giving the car the ability to hit 62 mph from a standstill in 3.4 seconds, on to a top speed of 193 mph (311 kph). A seven-speed PDK dual-clutch transmission is on deck to make sure the power is handled and used properly.
What makes the Porsche 911 GT3 Tribute to 911 GT1 special is, of course, the level of individualization it was subjected to, both inside and out. And nowhere is that more visible than in the way the body was specced.
It's the special livery that takes center stage. Designed in a way that reinterprets the one deployed on the winning GT1 30 years ago, the mostly white bodywork makes use of Club Blue, Jebsen Blue and Guards Red colors, highlighted by the Mobil 1 logo.
The visual impact the car has on the onlooker is further emphasized by the BBS Gold deployed on the forged magnesium wheels, which are based on the Weissach Package. Not only gold can be seen in there, as the rim borders have been painted in Brilliantchrome.
Photo: Porsche Fine touches and references can be seen almost everywhere. On the hood, the present-day Porsche crest has been replaced by the one that spelled Porsche 30 years ago. Then, inspired by the Manthey Kit for the GT3 RS, Porsche replaced the rear window with a carbon-fiber cover.
This element comes in white with a gold and black parallelogram pattern, and you'll find it nowhere else in this world, as it has been specifically imagined for this project. Finally, the words 'Born in Flacht' (Flacht is where Porsche Motorsport does its thing) are spelled in black on the rear apron, and an outline of the Zhuhai International Circuit can be seen on the rear wing end plates.
The Porsche 911 GT3 Tribute to 911 GT1 brings unique things to the table when it comes to the interior as well. The most noticeable fittings are the white trim strip (the same white as featured on the body) that runs the length of the dashboard and center console.
Porsche opted for Guards Red leather bucket seats for this project, with the seat belt pass-throughs finished in white. The door openers and the turnkey handle come in the same shade of red, something that Porsche has never done before on any of its vehicles.
Photo: Porsche The color was chosen, apparently, because it references the red interior details of the 1996 championship-winning GT1. And to really cement the connection between the two cars, the ‘Tribute to 911 GT1’ words are printed on the dashboard trim inlay and on the leather inlay on the floor mats. For kicks, Porsche wraps everything off with the 'Have Fun!' call to action written on the carbon-fiber door sill guards.
As it usually happens with such one-off projects, Porsche does not say how much it cost to put together. We also don't know what will happen to it now that it has been presented in the public for the first time.
It doesn't take a lot of effort, though, to imagine just how high the cost of the world's only Porsche of this kind could be. After all, the base car, the current-generation 911 GT3, goes for prices that start at around $235,000.
The German carmaker has four flavors of this car available for customers in the U.S.. The entry-level is the standard GT3, followed by the 911 GT3 with Touring Package and the 911 GT3 RS. As a twist, the special edition 911 GT3 90 F. A. Porsche is currently available as well, as a tribute to the man responsible for bringing the 911 nameplate to the world.

1966 Chrysler Imperial Has the Right Combo: Unrestored, All-Original, 440 Muscle
25 photos
Photo: eBay seller lubberbubberxlovebug
Unrestored. Original. The factory engine is still under the hood, and it’s even working. Is this enough to convince you to check out this 1966 Chrysler ? It should be.
This Imperial Crown four-door hardtop is a little piece of American car history, as it has never been touched or restored in any way. Everything you see on this car is exactly how Chrysler’s engineers wanted to be, so whoever refreshes it would better stick with the original configuration and not convert it into a custom abomination.
That’s why this Imperial is now here. It’s trying to sell, hoping that someone out there would have the resources and the courage to return it to its day-glory. It won’t be easy, especially if sticking to the all-original setup is the long-term objective.
Finding the necessary parts is more challenging than it looks because 1966 Imperials are not that common. Donors rarely make the headlines, and when they do, they come in ridiculous condition.
Photo: eBay seller lubberbubberxlovebug The Imperial didn’t receive any significant changes for the 1966 model year. The reason was the facelift that was introduced in 1964, and which completely transformed the car. This refresh worked like a charm in the following years, and Chrysler decided to stick with only subtle changes, such as the new grille introduced in 1966.
The Imperial continued to be offered in two configurations. The crown could be ordered as a two and a four-door hardtop plus a convertible, while the Lebaron was offered only as a four-door hardtop.
While the Imperial started the decade with a 413 V8 engine rated at 340 horsepower under the hood, this unit was upgraded for the 1966 model. This was actually the biggest change that happened in 1966, as the Imperial switched to a 440 engine that produced 350 horsepower.
Chrysler’s strategy worked, at least when the 1964 facelift came out. Sales increased almost overnight, with the company ending the year with 23,285 cars shipped to American buyers. Another overhaul followed in 1967.
Photo: eBay seller lubberbubberxlovebug The first thing that caught my attention when I first spotted this Chrysler was the solid body. It still looks clean and straight, but I wouldn’t actually make an offer without seeing it in person.
Sure, it doesn’t look restored, and that’s a plus, but you just ned to inspect everything for signs of rust. If possible, you should raise the Imperial on a lift to inspect the undersides and look for signs of previous repairs. The floors are typically the first ones to be invaded by rust, and without checking out every inch of metal thoroughly, you won’t be able to tell of sure if the car is as advertised.
If it passes the metal inspection, you should go on with a verification of the cabin. It shows its age, and the front seats will require urgent fixes.
I just wish we knew more about this car’s past because it doesn’t look like the owners babied it. The cabin is the living proof, as I can’t see how the front seats would end up in this shape if the car was parked in a garage and regularly started.
Photo: eBay seller lubberbubberxlovebug The owner insists that the photos you see in the gallery perfectly showcase the condition of the car today. They must be recent images, though they also leave some questions without an answer, especially the ones regarding the car’s past.
Otherwise, you’ll get good news when you open the hood. The engine hiding in there is a 440 – as I told you, the Imperial moved to a 440 beginning with the 1966 model year, so there’s a chance that this is the original configuration that was installed by Chrysler before the vehicle left the factory.
It runs and drives, and that’s fantastic news for someone who wants to drive this car during the restoration. However, it’s unclear if the vehicle is prepared for a long journey, and my recommendation is that you send your mechanic for an inspection because this is the only way to tell if flying in and driving home is possible.
Otherwise, you should also consider the shipping costs, which could be quite high, depending on where you live.
Photo: eBay seller lubberbubberxlovebug As for the selling price, this car isn’t expensive. The Imperial was a car whose maintenance was quite easy and affordable, but on the other hand, they burned a lot of fuel, which made sense, given the 440 engine under the hood.
They aren’t necessarily the most sought-after classics, but a collector would pay big bucks for a specimen that checks the right boxes (such as being all-original and in tip-top shape).
The owner wants $10,000 for this Imperial Crown, and they also enabled the Make Offer option on eBay, which is typically a sign that you might be able to get a discount if you’re committed to a fast purchase.
The car is parked in Yucca Valley, California, and a title is also included in the sale.

source_document.body:
Great on any Friday: NOCO Boost+Air AX65 - 2000A Jump Starter & Tire Inflator
Unrestored Mustang Needs a Home, It Doesn't Even Need a Complete Restoration
26 photos
Photo: eBay seller mustangbecky
Say what you want about the 1965 Mustang , but everybody knows what this car eventually represented in the American car space. This specimen is here to remind us of this, and more importantly, it does it in an unrestored condition.
This means that the Mustang you see in these pics has never been altered or restored, so most of the things you’ll end up discovering were last touched by Ford ’s engineers back in the day when it was still on the assembly line.
The car’s number one priority is to find a new home, with a small refresh then required to shine again as it did on day one. More importantly, a full restoration is not necessary in this case, and based on the photos and the data shared by the owner, overhauling this Mustang shouldn’t be too difficult.
Photo: eBay seller mustangbecky I’m pretty sure everybody remembers how the Mustang came to be, but one thing I want to highlight is that this car was never supposed to be expensive. Lee Iaccocca wanted the Mustang to cost only $2,500, and the final production model got even better than that.
The 6-cylinder hardtop coupe – the model that people aren’t necessarily interested in these days – could be had for only $2,320. It was an affordable price for people who wanted a daily driver, and the six-powered Mustang was certainly up to the task. The original 170ci engine offered on the 1964 1/2 models delivered only 101 horsepower, as its focus was specifically on offering an efficient ride.
The convertible carried a starting price tag of $2,557, while the 2+2 fastback rolled out with a similar price tag - $2,553 – in September.
Ford knew that not everybody wanted an efficient ride, as the muscle under the hood was still a big thing back then. That’s why it launched a high-performance 289 rated at 271 horsepower in June 1964.
However, most people decided to stick with the base V8s – originally, this was a 260 with 164 horsepower, but when the 1965 model year stepped in, it was upgraded to a 289. A four-barrel version of the same engine was also offered.
Photo: eBay seller mustangbecky While a Hi-Po would have been a fantastic engine on this Mustang, especially considering it has never been restored, that’s not what you’ll find under its hood.
It still has a V8, but a regular 289 paired with an automatic transmission. It starts, runs, drives, you name it, and considering the car has never been restored, it should be safe to assume that this engine has never been rebuilt either.
I would still ask my mechanic to inspect what happens under the hood before anything else, as I don’t think that getting a 1965 Mustang without the original engine under the hood would make sense if the price weren’t the right one.
Otherwise, this Mustang certainly looks like a small piece of automotive history. It still wears the factory paint, and despite showing its age, with some obvious cracks that might be easier to notice during an in-person inspection, it’s still in good shape.
I wish we knew more about this Mustang because the condition of the paint and the unrestored shape suggest that the car has been babied throughout its entire life, and I wouldn’t be surprised to learn that it’s a family-owned specimen. Just ask all these questions during your live inspection because you could end up coming across quite a gem.
The interior is also in good shape and also original.
Photo: eBay seller mustangbecky The cabin also shows its age, but I think this is something we can ignore, considering it has never been refreshed. The car comes with air conditioning – still blowing cold – and power steering.
The rust isn’t a concern on this Mustang, and the owner says the car is as clean as possible. If possible, you should raise it on a lift and inspect the undersides because an unrestored pile of metal born in 1965 is very unlikely to escape without at least surface corrosion.
Otherwise, I expect this Mustang to find a new home quite fast if – and this is a big if – it's priced correctly.
Photo: eBay seller mustangbecky The owner believes that $18,500 is a fair expectation for an unrestored Mustang, but they also enabled the Make Offer option on eBay. This is an opportunity to discuss the price if you are committed to a purchase, and considering 21 people have already added the vehicle to their watchlists, you might some competition this time.
The listing is set to expire in 19 days, unless someone clicks the Buy It Now button earlier. Otherwise, if you want to see this Mustang in person, you must call the seller and then pack your bags for a trip to Dumas, Arkansas.
Considering its shape, it should be able to move on its own, so you won’t need to pay for shipping to your garage, especially if you don’t live far from this location.

Great on any Friday: Apple USB-C Woven Cable - 3ft, 60W, White
Someone Bought This Ford Thunderbird in 2002 and Parked It. 24 Years Later, It Has 29 Miles
29 photos
Photo: Cars and Bids
To make a long story short, this 2002 Ford Thunderbird was driven off the showroom floor, parked in a climate-controlled garage, and never touched again. Now, the car is out in broad daylight, sitting at the dealership and ready to find another owner.
Just 29.3 miles or 47.15 kilometers. This is how far this 2002 Ford Thunderbird has traveled since it rolled off the production line. It wasn’t even taken out for maintenance because at that sort of mileage, it hasn't required any. Everything is original on the car, including the tires. So whoever buys this Thunderbird will have to change them ASAP if they are planning to drive it.
The car is finished in black with a matching removable hardtop and a black soft top over an interior with seats wrapped in black leather upholstery, and rides on 17-inch chrome wheels. Dual-zone automatic climate control and an in-dash CD changer are also on board.
The list of factory equipment is quite short because there is no sign of the window sticker, and the dealer can't figure out on its own everything the car came with. We can safely assume that the owner who sold it to the selling dealer back in August also had trouble remembering. There is no backstory and no plot twist on this car, even though low-mileage models always have a story to tell.
Photo: Cars and Bids What we do know is that there is a 3.9-liter Jaguar-derived V8 engine under the hood. It makes 252 horsepower (256 metric horsepower) and 267 pound-feet (362 Newton meters) of torque. That is enough for a run from 0 to 60 mph (0 to 97 kph) in 6.8 seconds on its way to a top speed of 130 mph (209 kph).
A 5R55N five-speed automatic transmission puts the power down through the rear wheels. Ford never offered a manual transmission with the 11th generation of the Thunderbird, even though the automaker was well aware that it would have brought out the car's sportier side. It did, however, offer the 55R55S with manual gear-selection controls.
Built on a shortened rear-wheel-drive platform shared with the Lincoln LS and Jaguar S-Type, it was anything but a sports car. It was actually more of a smooth operator, designed and engineered to prioritize cruising and comfort over sharp handling.
When Ford revived the Thunderbird for 2002, after a five-year hiatus, initial demand was high enough that dealers marked them up and collectors stashed them away, expecting rapid appreciation. The Ford Thunderbird hit the market with a starting MSRP of $35,495, destination charges included, for the base Deluxe convertible and climbed to $41,995 for the limited-run Neiman Marcus Edition.
Photo: Cars and Bids But because initial demand far exceeded supply across the 2001 and 2002 production years, many Ford dealers charged $5,000 to $15,000 over MSRP, pushing real-world transaction prices past $50,000. Such numbers pushed it into the same segment as the BMW Z3 Roadster, Chrysler Prowler, Mercedes-Benz SLK , and Chevrolet Corvette Convertible.
This is what probably convinced collectors to buy them and park them, hoping to cash in one day. That is exactly why a very low-mileage example hits the market every once in a while. Ford built 31,368 Thunderbirds for the 2002 model year. That single year accounted for roughly 46% of the entire 2002 - 2005 eleventh-generation production run of 68,098 cars total.
However, some owners must have waited far too long to sell. On the collector car market, a 2002 Ford Thunderbird typically sells for $12,000 to $18,000 in clean, driver-grade condition, while ultra-low-mileage, time-capsule examples, such as this one, reach $26,000 to $35,000. So nobody’s getting rich selling nowadays.
With four days to go, the highest bid reached $17,250. There is still time. The future owner will get a car with a clean Carfax report with no accidents or mileage discrepancies (who would’ve thought?). They will also go home with a key and a fob, the hardtop rack, and the factory cover. No window sticker is available and, of course, there are zero service records for the car that never left the garage.
Photo: Cars and Bids From the moment this 2002 Ford Thunderbird goes home with someone else, the future owner has two options. They can park it in another climate-controlled garage and wait for the moment the collector car market is kinder to the model, and they will be able to fetch more than they paid for it.
Or they can just drive it until its wheels fall off, even though the car’s value would instantly drop. On roads where everybody drives pickup trucks and SUVs, this would really be a showstopper. It has stayed parked and hidden long enough.
This may look like the lowest-mileage Thunderbird on the face of the earth, but it is not. Another time capsule 2002 model, finished in Evening Black, surfaced back in 2026 with just 15 delivery miles (24.1 kilometers), beating the 29-mile car by 14 miles (22.5 kilometers).

Cupra Launches ABT-Tuned Raval and Leon in the UK, Here's How Much the New Range-Toppers Cost
9 photos
Photo: Cupra UK
Cupra and ABT Sportsline continue their collaboration by introducing modded versions of the Raval and the Leon in the United Kingdom.
Following in the footsteps of the Cupra Formentor VZ ABT , which launched earlier this month (November 2026), the two models are called the Cupra Raval VZ ABT and the Leon VZ ABT.
Pricing starts from 36,995 pounds (equal to $48,430) for the Cupra Raval VZ ABT, which is said to be eligible for a 1,500 pounds ($1,965) ECG (Electric Car Grant) discount. As for the Leon VZ ABT, it starts at 48,510 pounds ($63,505) OTR, and it obviously sits at the top of the family, above the previous range-topper, namely the VZ, which kicks off at 45,370 pounds ($62,015) locally.
Lesser versions of the Cupra Leon (Hatch) include the Shadow Edition, V2, and V1, and these can be ordered from 37,540 pounds ($49,145), 34,475 pounds ($45,130), and 32,580 pounds ($42,650), respectively. As for the Raval lineup, it kicks off from 25,495 pounds ($32,065) for the V1, and also includes the V2, VZ, and VZ Extreme, priced from 28,080 pounds ($36,760), 34,495 pounds ($45,160), and 34,810 pounds ($45,570), respectively. The Raval Origin will join the family in 2027.
Photo: Cupra UK Announced during the Paris Motor Show earlier this year, the VZ ABT is pretty much a styling package that was developed in partnership between Cupra and ABT Sportsline. The automaker and the renowned tuner say that the bundle comprises several hand-fitted exterior enhancements. These include stuff such as the skirts at the front and rear, as well as the side skirt add-ons, a distinctive roof spoiler, and subtle winglets at both ends.
No tuning job would be complete these days without a set of aftermarket wheels, and the VZ ABT versions of the Cupra Raval and Leon also tick this box. The company says that the alloys of choice in this case are called the ICON. They measure 19 inches in diameter, are presented in matte black, and feature ABT branding on them in order to make them more recognizable.
It is definitely worth noting that each Custom Cupra by ABT pack is equipped by hand at the Cupra Racing Factory, and it is a great way to make your Raval or Leon, or the Formentor, for that matter, which starts at 54,125 pounds ($70,855) OTR in the United Kingdom. The latter comes with a 2-liter four-pot making 333 ps (328 hp/245 kW).
Cupra’s Formentor VZ5 ABT is also available in the UK, packing the Audi Sport-sourced 2.5-liter five-banger that develops 390 ps (385 hp/287 kW), and kicks off at 66,420 pounds ($86,950). The regular non-ABT Formentor also comes in the VZ5, VZ, V2, and V1 trim levels, and it starts at 64,495 pounds ($84,430), 48,455 pounds ($63,435), 37,875 pounds ($49,585), and 35,530 pounds ($46,515), respectively, the automaker’s official local website reveals.

2027 Toyota 4Runner Adventure SUV Becomes More Expensive and Only Adds a Few Perks to Compensate
23 photos
Photo: Toyota
The Japanese automaker Toyota is continuing its long string of updates for various markets and regions; now it's a bit more focused on America – the United States, to be more precise.
We’re thankful because the company is making updates across the board: over in the United Kingdom, the new Lexus TZ arrives as a premium Toyota Highlander starting from no less than £74,895, which is the equivalent of almost $98k at the current exchange rates – that’s quite a lump sum for the new electric crossover.
Over at home in Japan, Toyota just welcomed the XV80 Toyota Camry Hybrid made in the United States into the lineup – it arrives in the Land of the Rising Sun after a three-year hiatus on the market, but at least it costs a lot less than the TZ. In fact, the base Camry G model starts at ¥4,300,000, which is just $27k cheaper than the American Camry, which kicks off at an MSRP of $29,700 sans destination!
Back in America, Toyota just updated the best-selling Tacoma mid-size pickup truck to the 2027 model year credentials, featuring mostly the same stuff as before along with a minor $180 price bump. Well, now it’s time for the SUV sibling to also come out to play, with the 2027 4Runner also on the upgrade roll call.
This time around, the base MSRP jump is way more consistent: a 2026 Toyota 4Runner kicks off at $42,270 sans destination, while the newer 2027MY goes from $43,490. That’s pretty massive, if you ask us, especially when the updates are also minor, just like with the Tacoma. But hey, the adventure SUV might be a victim of its own success and corporate greed, as the sales have jumped massively in recent months.
Anyway, the novelties for the 2027 Toyota 4Runner series include additional “standard comfort on core grades—highlighted by newly standard heated and power-adjustable front seats—while TRD Pro adds standard red tow hooks and the distinctive new exclusive color Hot Honey.” The heated front seats and eight-way power front driver and passenger seats, at least, are standard across all trim levels.
Also, alongside the TRD Pro-exclusive color Hot Honey, there’s a new black hue, too, called Inked. For the 2027 model year, the 4Runner soldiers on with the same powertrains – a turbocharged 2.4-liter four-cylinder engine paired with an eight-speed automatic transmission offered in two versions. The ICE setup has 78 horsepower and 317 lb-ft of torque, while the hybrid system has a combined 326 hp and 465 lb-ft of torque.
The 4Runner is produced on Toyota’s TNGA-F global body-on-frame truck platform, shared with the Tacoma and Land Cruiser, among others. It comes with many off-road features, including part- or full-time four-wheel drive systems, electronic locking differential, Multi-Terrain Select, Crawl Control, a stabilizer-bar Disconnect Mechanism (SDM), skid plates, off-road-tuned suspension parts, and all-terrain tires.
